text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to our board meeting of October, I'm sorry, October, April, April 28, 2026. And as the board knows, we only have one agenda item today. But before we go to that agenda item, we are going to begin this meeting, as we always do, which is with a moment of silence to be followed by the Pledge of Allegiance.

And before I ask those who are able to rise, I do want us to keep in our thoughts and prayers Senator Mark Warner and his family. As we all know, it's with profound sadness that we learned the passing of Madison Warner, the daughter of Senator Mark Warner, at the way too early age of 36. And Madison passed away after a decades-long battle with juvenile diabetes and other health issues. And this, obviously, is a very difficult moment for the senator and his wife, Lisa, to be

in this position as parents. And we want to extend our heartfelt condolences to Senator Warner and his family. And I will mention that since the very first day I met Senator Warner, he's been talking about and advocating for cures and treatment for juvenile diabetes. And this hits personal for him, but I think it's just another tragedy, unfortunately, in a series of tragedies we've had in our community lately. And if we could keep Mark Warner in our thoughts and prayers, that would be appreciated by by me and I know he would appreciate hearing that from residents of Fairfax County during this tough time and if there's others

who would like to be recognized for remembrances let me recognize Supervisor Jimenez thank you Mr. Chairman I'd like to take a moment to recognize the passing of John H. Hawes a longtime resident of our community in Mason district who passed away on April 3rd 2026 at the age of 84 Mr. Hawes lived a life defined by public service, intellectual curiosity, and a deep commitment to education.

A graduate of Princeton University, John went on to serve our nation for three decades as a Foreign Service Officer with the United States Department of State. His work took him across the globe, where he played a role in advancing diplomacy. Following his distinguished federal career, Mr. Hawes continued his service closer to home as an educator in Fairfax County Public Schools.

At Annandale High School, he inspired students through the International Bachelorette Program, earning recognition as Teacher of the Year and leaving a lasting impact on countless young people, including some of who worked alongside him after graduating.

I would like to extend our county's condolences to his family, friends, former colleagues, and students. His legacy of service and education will continue to benefit our community for years to come. Thank you, Mr. Chairman. Thank you, Supervisor Jimenez, for that announcement. Seeing and hearing no other board members, if all who are able to, could rise for a moment of silence to be followed by the Pledge of Allegiance.
And as I mentioned earlier, this meeting of the Board of Supervisors is for our budget markup for fiscal year 2027.

And as the board knows, there are a number of actions that we'll be taking this morning, and I ask everyone for their patience with me. There's a lot to read here. Everyone should have the package in front of them. And we'll begin with the approval of the FY2026 third quarter review.

And at this time, I am going to hand the gavel to Vice Chairman Smith, as I'll be making a number of motions. First, the FY2026 third quarter review, as advertised, included previous balances of $52 million and recommended revenue spending and reserve adjustments totaling a net of $50.3 million, with a majority proposed for investments in capital paydown, information technology projects, and support for the county's parks.

The advertised budget included a net balance available to the Board of Supervisors of $1.7 million, roughly. The board utilizes this balance to provide additional funding to the county's Reserve for Economic Uncertainty, which was established as part of the FY2026 budget to respond to changing economic conditions.

I would further add that this reserve is not only for further economic conditions, but obviously to address a lot of the chaos that is happening in Washington, D.C. This action reflects our commitment to maintaining fiscal resilience and ensuring that the county is prepared to respond to potential revenue fluctuations or emerging needs.

And so you can see in the chart there, the FY2026 third quarter board adjustment sends the entire remaining balance into our reserve for economic uncertainty. Therefore, I move approval of the FY2026 third quarter review, including approval of Supplemental Appropriation Resolution AS 26190, an amendment to the Fiscal Planning Resolution AS 26901, which include the revenue expenditure and transfer adjustments, grant awards and adjustments, and associated reserve adjustments contained in the counties and schools' third quarter review, dated March 17, 2026,

and the appropriation of $2 million from the fuel reserve as recommended in the add-on package dated April 16, 2026, and the board adjustments listed above, which result in a net balance of zero. I'll second that motion along with Supervisor Palachuk.

Discussion on the motion, Mr. Chairman? No discussion. I would just suggest that, you know, again, this is sending the remaining balance, which is small, into our reserve for economic uncertainty, and clearly, I think we all know we're living in extraordinarily uncertain times as we deal with not only the chaos in Washington, D.C., but rising fuel costs, inflationary, and tariff impacts on so many residents in Fairfax County, and this is a proven action, and I'd appreciate the board's support.

Thank you. Supervisor Herity? Well, I just know it's not just the $1.6 million. There's a whole list of spending items that the county executive, the only change that's being made, which I support and I like, is the $1.6 million.

Correct. So I just want to make sure taxpayers know that there is a list of spending besides just taking the $1.6 million that's left over and putting it there. Right, and, of course, that was reflected in what I read. Okay, seeing no further discussion, all those in favor of the motion, please say aye.

Aye. Anyone opposed? Parity, nay. Any abstentions? That motion carries at a 9-1 vote. Mr. Chairman. Thank you very much. At this time, we move into the FY 2027 budget markup, and I will outline and move approval of the budget proposal.

This package begins with a balance of $23.17 million, which represents the balance included in the advertised budget, and no adjustments impacting this balance were recommended in the county executive's add-on package which was sent out April 16, 2026. And I'm going to begin with adjustments recommended by the board. The board appreciates the diligent and disciplined approach taken by the county executive in developing the FY 2027 advertised budget plan under challenging circumstances. The continued economic and political uncertainty created by the

current federal administration has made long-term planning more difficult for residents, businesses, and local governments alike. Despite these headwinds, the county executive put forward a balanced budget that does not require an increase in the real estate tax rate. Navigating these challenges without raising the real estate tax rate has required a fourth consecutive year of agency budget reductions, with this sustained effort to control costs now totaling approximately $124 million. In addition, the proposed budget included a comprehensive review of fees, such as those in our land development process.

At the same time, the board appreciates the emphasis on our workforce with fully funding of the collective bargaining agreements with the county's three unions and equitable increases for non-represented employees that include pay scale adjustments to maintain internal equity between the S, M, and A scales.

We also value the investment that this budget makes in our facilities, recognizing both the importance of safe, well-maintained infrastructure today and the need for continued investment in the years ahead. The proposed budget allocated just over 51 percent of the county's budget, or over $3 billion to the Fairfax County public schools. The state has yet to finalize its budget. However, we remain optimistic that our state partners will step up to the plate and increase their support of K-12 education. In addition to operating support, the county's

budget strengthens our investment in schools infrastructure, reflecting our shared challenges of aging facilities and deferred maintenance. Continued collaboration on capital planning and facility renewal will be essential to ensure both county and school buildings remain safe, functional, and able to support the wide array of services our residents and students rely on.

The board's markup to the FY 2027 budget builds on the county executive's proposal to reducing the real estate tax rate by a further quarter penny from the current rate of $112 and a quarter penny per $100 of assessed value to $112 even per $100 of assessed value. At the current tax rate, the impact on the average real estate tax bill would have been $357. With this rate reduction, the average increase is reduced to $337. The board is acutely aware of the financial pressures and

uncertainty many residents continue to face and believes it is important to moderate the impact on homeowners where possible. This reduction is made possible in large part due to the impact of the food and beverage tax on the county's budget, which has begun to deliver on its intended purpose of diversifying our revenue base, lessening our reliance on the real estate tax, and allowing some of the cost of county programs to be shared by visitors, commuters, and others who spend money in Fairfax County, but do not pay property taxes here. In developing this markup package, the board also carefully considered the concerns raised by residents about several programs that were

recommended for full elimination. We recognize that achieving the necessary savings in this budget involves difficult choices and that these reductions are not without pain for the communities and individuals who rely on these services. However, in response to community input and with a focus on aligning resources with actual utilization, the board is partially restoring funding for four programs, $250,000 for the low and moderate income home repair pilot, $200,000 for the contract providing a part-time preschool program, $130,588 for home-delivered

meals, and $310,000 for the Be Well program. These targeted restorations will allow these programs to continue in a right-sized form while still operating within a more efficient footprint. Where reductions remain, such as for our community centers, the board expects that staff will work with our nonprofit partners to ensure a seamless transition of services.

The board is also deferring by one year the planned realignment of transition services provided to high school seniors with individualized education plans who are leaving FCPS and moving into adulthood. While these services remain more appropriately aligned with FCPS, This change will now be implemented as part of the FY 2028 budget rather than the upcoming fiscal year.

This deferral will provide FCPS with additional time to prepare for and assume this function, ensuring a smooth transition for students and families. Two of my recent board matters directed staff to advance the board's priorities related to economic competitiveness and attainable housing.

The recommendations emerging from these initiatives will require additional staff capacity to implement. To support the Housing Task Force and related work, the Board is creating one new position in Land Development Services, LDS, funded entirely by LDS revenues with no cost to the general fund.

In addition, one new position will be added to the Department of Economic Initiatives to support the county's economic competitiveness efforts. The cost of this position will be largely offset by abolishing a vacant position in the Office of the Commonwealth's Attorney, reflecting the Board's continued commitment to aligning resources with priority initiatives while minimizing the impact on taxpayers.

Affordable housing remains a major priority for the Board of Supervisors, and we continue to take deliberate steps toward our goal of a minimum of 10,000 new affordable homes. As part of this markup package, the board is allocating the equivalent of additional quarter penny on the real estate tax rate, or roughly $8.8 million to affordable housing.

This brings our recurring baseline investment in affordable housing to a penny and a half on the real estate tax rate or $52.7 million, providing a predictable, ongoing investment in affordable housing and reflecting our commitment to sustained progress on this critical community need.

The remaining balance of $4,676,495 is allocated to the Reserve for Economic Uncertainty. Given the continued volatility and unpredictability associated with the current federal administration and broader economic conditions, the Board believes it is prudent to bolster this reserve as a safeguard against potential revenue shortfalls or emerging expenditure pressures.

Strengthening the reserve for economic uncertainty enhances the county's ability to respond quickly and responsibly to changing circumstances while helping to preserve critical services and maintain stability for our residents, businesses, and employees.

And everything that I've just outlined, you can see in the chart, which shows you all the adjustments that are being made. And as a result of these changes, we have a balanced FY 2027 budget. This budget includes other tax and fee adjustments, including decreases to the following taxes.

A decrease in the Route 28 Highway Transportation Improvement District tax from a rate of $0.12 to $0.10.5 per $100 of assessed value. A decrease in the Phase 2 Dulles Rail Transportation Improvement Tax District from a rate of $0.14 to $0.12 per $100 of assessed value.

Increases are included in land use, refuse, and sewer charges as follows. an increase in the refuse collection fee from $610 to $630 per household, an increase in the refuse disposal fee from $90 to $98 per ton, an increase in the sewer service charges from $9.33 to $9.88 per 1,000 gallons, an increase in the sewer service base charge from $5,262 to $55.78 per quarter, an increase in the sewer availability charge from $9,218 to $9,398.

Taxes and fees in the FY2027 budget that remain unchanged include the leaf collection rate, which remains at $0.019 per $100 of assessed value, the stormwater sewer services tax district, which remains at $0.0325 per $100 of assessed value, The Phase I Dulles Rail Transportation Improvement District Tax, which remains at $0.09 per $100 of assessed value.
The Reston Service District Tax Rate, which remains at $0.021 per $100 of assessed value. The Tyson Service District Tax Rate, which remains at $0.05 per $100 of assessed value.

Therefore, having provided public notice and conducted a public hearing as required by Virginia law, I move approval of the FY 2027 budget as advertised with the changes included in the add-on package dated April 16, 2026, and as outlined above, and required managed reserve adjustments.

The tax and fee adjustments become effective on and after July 1, 2026, unless otherwise noted. These actions result in a balanced budget for FY 2027. I'll second that motion. Discussion on the motion, Mr. Chairman?

Thank you very much, Vice Chairman Smith, and I may have further discussion later, but I do want to thank the public and members of this board for their participation in this year's budget process. As folks know, we heard from thousands of people, certainly I did across the county, and this budget reflects the lion's share of those interests that we heard throughout the process, whether that was in sustaining some of the core programs that were reduced in the county executive's budget, or whether that was to reduce the tax rate, which this budget does by a quarter of a penny.

I would say that, you know, budgets are, we often look at budgets as a statement of our values, and I feel strongly about that. But I also believe that as supervisors, it is our role to vote on budgets in their totality.

And so I will tell you, and I've told my colleagues and others this, that not everything in this budget do I agree with. But that's not really what the question is. It's not whether you agree with everything in this budget. It's whether this budget in its totality, does that reflect what we consider to be the will of the residents that we support.

And I believe it does that, both in balancing a reduction in the tax rate, but also looking for structural savings within the county budget, which this clearly does, and most importantly, sets aside money in reserves in Fairfax County, which are all completely and totally funded due to a lot of work by this board over a lot of years to get to a point where our reserves are fully funded.

And anyone who pays attention to what's going on in the news understands that there's potentially no place further impacted in the country by what's happening in Washington, D.C., than Northern Virginia. And if you look at what's happened in Maryland and D.C. with their credit ratings, we take our AAA bond rating here very seriously.

and we do not want to succumb to the fiscal challenges that are significantly occurring throughout the DMV, but that while we are feeling the effects of those, we certainly don't want to position our county budget in any manner that would undermine the fiscal and financial stability of this county that not only our residents rely on, but our businesses rely on as well.

This budget makes a significant investment in Fairfax County public schools, as we always do, knowing how important they are to the future financial success of the county. I mentioned in my motion, long motion, that there are a lot of positions that are cut in this budget, and I appreciate the county executive, the work that he did throughout the course of the last year to come forward with a package that restructures and creates savings within the county budget.

And I would say that this board, contrary to what some say, this board works on the budget every single day of the calendar year. Not in the weeks leading up to the budget, not with special task forces, but we work on the budget every single day.

Every single committee meeting of this board, I consider to be a subcommittee of the budget committee. Because every time we meet throughout the year, we are giving advice to county staff about how we want money and resources spent, what programs we support, and we, of course, vet those heavily throughout the entire calendar year.

This is not a job where you show up, participate in public hearings for two weeks, and then say terrible things about the budget. This is a job that requires board members to show up throughout the year to vet budget proposals and to vet our resources as we head towards budget adoption.

And so while today is a big day in terms of the budget calendar structurally, for me it's just another day of making sure that we prepare our county for challenges ahead, but also maintain and govern the largest county in Virginia, which requires a hands-on approach to our fiscal affairs every single day.

And so I would appreciate my colleagues' support for this budget. Again, I think each one of us would find things in this budget we would have done a little bit differently. But the motion that I made reflects the consensus of the board in my conversations with every member of this board.

But I also think most, in a most demonstrated way, also reflects the priorities of our residents and the people that we heard from throughout the calendar year leading up to today. Finally, you know, we always look at budgets in the year that we're doing them, but we look ahead to the year ahead.

And I am hopeful that next year we're able to continue on this path of providing tax relief and savings to our residents. I'll just close by saying it is not lost on me that our residents are feeling the daily effects of absolute chaos that is occurring around them.

Four plus dollar a gallon gasoline, inflation, tariffs, wars, reductions to federal programs, reductions to our federal workforce and contractors. There's not a place I can go in the county where people in this county are not suffering right now because of policies that are being pursued at the federal level.

We have to take that into account, and I am hopeful next year that our General Assembly and Governor will continue to make big investments in public education to help relieve the real estate tax burden on residents of Fairfax County. The reduction that is in my proposed motion is largely there to the tax rate as a result of the meals tax and the revenue that's coming in on the meals tax, and I hope that continues to provide real estate tax relief in the years ahead because the two most important things for next year's budget will be state support for public education, which is the lion's share of

our budget, and diversification so that we can continue, in my hope, continue to reduce the real estate tax rate on residents in Fairfax County. And so I look forward to the conversation and would appreciate my colleague's support. Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I have Supervisor Alcorn.

Thank you very much, Madam Chair. Just a brief statement. I do appreciate all the work that's gone into this and all the work you, Mr. Chairman, have done and also the staff. I did say at the beginning of the budget process, at least this part of the budget process, that I would be watching for and listening carefully for the impacts on our most vulnerable.

And I have listened, and I've come to the conclusion I cannot support a reduction of the real estate tax rate, even a small amount, while also cutting services across several programs to some of our most vulnerable residents. So I will be voting no on this markup motion. Thank you.

Thank you, Supervisor Alcorn, Supervisor Pelczyk, Herity, and then Lusk. Thank you, Madam Vice Chair. I do have slightly longer comments, but I really appreciate the work of all of my colleagues. But especially I want to thank the chairman, his leadership and his approach to a difficult budget, and 10 different points of view on that budget, I know is not an easy task.

And while none of us had everything we wanted, I feel that overall we have the right emphasis on this budget, especially gone through the weeks of public hearing and hearing from our community. I believe the changes to the budget represent a balance of improving affordability for homeowners and renters while implementing targeted restorations to essential human services programs.

We're able to transfer more funds to schools than we ever have before and are hopeful that when the General Assembly finally passes its budget, there will be additional funding for education. As was mentioned, the diversification of county tax revenue has created a buffer, enabling us to reduce the property tax rate while still maintaining investments in important county initiatives.

For me, the housing affordability crisis is top of mind. As we put forward this budget, our budget is a representation of our values, and too many are left with inadequate housing options in our county, jeopardizing our long-term economic outlook as well. Just a few facts on that. In the rental market, Fairfax County has 59,000 cost-burdened renter households, paying more than 45% of their income on housing. And the increase in rent has outpaced increases in income, rents increasing by 5% on average, while incomes increase

by 2%. On the home ownership side, it should bring us all pause that home ownership is so out of reach for working families and young professionals hoping to plant roots or stay here in Fairfax County. Buyers aged 25 to 34 have made up just 7 to 10% of all homeowners since 2010. Over the last decade, we've added 2.3 new jobs per new home. With this in mind, the county will need to add at least 41,000 new homes by 2035. I believe the increase in funding of a quarter penny to the

county's affordable housing fund represents a meaningful step in moving us forward in our goal to reach two pennies for the dollar annually to accomplish our goal of 10,000 affordable homes by 2034. This additional commitment to the housing authority allows us to continue making loans to support affordable housing development projects in the existing pipeline and to capitalize on immediate strategic acquisition opportunities that have emerged in the market, and it solidifies our commitments to shovel-ready projects like the construction of Tyson Central, East County,

and Dulles Green across the county. We have also made targeted restorations to programs that support our most vulnerable. All Ages Read Together, that serves the ALIS population, those who are asset-limited, income-constrained, and employed, providing supplemental education opportunities.

The Home Improvement Pilot Program for seniors and adults with disabilities, Home Delivered Programs for seniors, and Be Well, a program that helps connect those that receive CSB support to access primary care and preventive health programs. All of these programs continue to show promising results in how they're supporting residents at every stage of life.

But there's more work to be done to measure their impact and gauge how they fit into the county's web of supportive services. Through this budget, we'll continue to push forward our goals as a county, and I'm happy to see the adjustments that we have collaborated on through this process. And while we are hopeful when the General Assembly passes its budget, they will do their part in supporting education here in Virginia, we know that so much of that is here on the backs of our residents in Fairfax County.

Finally, I want to thank our County Executive, Brian Hill, his team, our CFO, Christina, and everyone on the budget team, Phil and all those here, for their work, to my colleagues, and most of all to the constituents and the organizations that have thoughtfully made their voices heard, whether here in person or reaching out directly to us. And I'm very, very happy to support the chairman's proposed budget. Thank you. I have Supervisor Herity, then Lusk, then Stork.

Apologize, I'm going to be a little longer, but I want to start by thanking our staff, management and budget, the county executive. I know there were a lot of questions that were submitted and a lot of work done to get us some of the answers. Also want to thank our employees who took the time to submit 872 suggestions on how the budget could be improved.

It is truly unfortunate because of collective bargaining that we were not even able to look at those suggestions and consider them in the budget. And I hope that issue gets resolved soon because I think our employees have a lot to offer here. But here we go again, we're at line item cuts.

With all due respect to the chairman, we talk about doing the budget every day. This board knows that I consistently ask, what is the fiscal impact when we adopt policies? And most often those policies come without fiscal impacts, and you're going to hear later about some of those fiscal impacts, not all of them, but one or two of them.

My main issue with this budget is affordability. Budgets are about priorities, and our taxpayers have not been a priority. Taxes are up 60% over 10 years. They're too high, and we've added a meals tax. The $20 tax credit that the quarter penny gives our residents doesn't cut it because their taxes are still going up, and they've got the meals tax.

The chairman mentioned the $124 million in agency budget reductions proposed by the county executive. What wasn't mentioned is that these reductions were offset by significant increase in spending, spending driven by board policies and priorities.

So it's clear to taxpayers the general fund did not go down by $124 million. It went up by $868 million over those four years. They were reductions to partly offset significant increases. The board promised the meals tax would offset real estate tax increases, But what it has done is reduce the increase necessary to keep up with additional spending.

Tax bills are still going up despite the meals tax and the small reduction in the rate. Some reductions identified by the county executive and staff are good. And some of those were recommendations of mine last year, including the Commonwealth attorney position vacancies, streamlining agency functions in a couple of agencies.

Some reductions are not good in being made to longstanding staples of our community. The Golden Gazette, which is a small cost to share information, the Meals on Wheels reductions, high school crossing guards, I mean, it's a good idea for staff to look, and I'm happy we're looking at outsourcing.

However, I'm completely disappointed with the way this has been handled. We're still missing feedback from principals, bus driver leads, FCPS transportation. The number, the reduction number, is wrong. I never got an answer out of that budget committee.

What I hear from parents, principals, bus drivers, commuters that drive past, that live in school zones, is that we're having issues with the bus driver pilot. We're going to need to do more work on that. Glad to see we're forcing a commitment to the middle school after school program.

There are also needs that I don't think are adequately addressed in this budget. The library collection, sheriff deputies pay. You know, we have a real issue in the sheriff's department, and we've talked about it at this dais for over two years, and now we're going to fund a study, and we know what happens when we fund a study.

It's going to be another year, and we're way past the need for increases in our sheriff's department. Their numbers show it. You can actually get a cost savings by offsetting some overtime. I don't understand why that wasn't addressed in this budget.

Increased maintenance funding, as I have been talking about, county parks, schools. On the county side, many of our Category F projects still go unfunded. We've got a maintenance backlog of over $200 million. Base IT funding.

It's too late to solve this when we get to the budget process. We can't lie down and cut our way to an affordable budget. For years, you've heard me say deep dive on the budget. I don't care what you call it. It's a strategic look. It gets outside help.

It doesn't just mean looking at our budget strategically. It looks looking at our policies strategically. What are the fiscal impacts of the policies that are baked into the budget? Let me just give you an example, the energy investments that have unintended consequences, and I don't know if you saw the budget answer to this, so I'm going to read part of it.

Modern critical building systems related to implementation of the county's community-wide energy and climate action plan, CCAP, and zero carbon initiatives are significantly more complex than those installed 20 to 30 years ago.

And that complexity directly translates into higher maintenance costs. More energy efficiency has introduced advanced technologies that, while beneficial in the long-term for operational environmental performance, require ongoing calibration, software updates, and more frequent preventive maintenance. These systems are less tolerant of failure and more interdependent, meaning a single fault can impact multiple building functions.

This evolution towards more complex energy efficient infrastructure is a key driver of rising maintenance expenditures. It shifts the cost profile from basic repairs to specialized technology-driven maintenance and support. We had to replace the entire lighting system at the Sharon Boulevard CSB building. I mean, the entire lighting system, and it wasn't built that long ago. Our policies are driving up costs, and when it gets to this dais, I ask about the cost impact.

You've heard me, and often we go forward without understanding the cost impact. Another way to look strategically at the cost driver is our health insurance costs are going up. There are simple ways to encourage our employees to get physicals with financial incentives. It's the number one thing industry is doing to reduce health care costs. We can better educate our employees and not just sending emails but going out and meeting with them about the advantages to them of health savings account because it gets consumers involved in health care. These are simple things that we

can do if we look at the budget strategically. Another is pension costs for general county employees, not public safety, just general county employees, they add 34 cents to every payroll dollar. For those that haven't been keeping track, that's up from 20 cents to every payroll dollar since 2015. I'm very proud of the two rounds of pension reform work the board accomplished some years ago, and we still have an above-market pension plan for our general county employees.

That number would be higher today if not for those reforms, and I want to make a key point here because I got accused of trying to take people's pension benefits away. We did that without taking away pension benefits for existing employees. And any pension reform I'm ever involved with, we won't be taking benefits away from employees that currently have them.

Several years ago, then-Supervisor Walkinshaw asked about investment returns and administration costs on our pensions. The board commissioned and funded a study of our pension returns and pension administration. That review was completed in September of 2024, but to my knowledge, the review results and recommendations have not been formally delivered to or discussed by this board.

We always say personnel costs are a major driver of the budget. Well, pension costs are 33% to 60% on top of those costs and have been increasing. Have we delved into why and what we could do about it?

At the same time, according to the budget question we received just before 5 last night, They indicate that they're not important to recruiting or retention. So for most firms, most companies, 33% is their entire fringe benefit package.

Sick, vacation, holiday, health insurance, life insurance, FICA, FUTA. For us, it's just the pension costs, and it's gone up from 20% to 33%. We need to understand those costs. That report makes some significant recommendations that don't touch benefits.

They address administration and the fact that our returns significantly lag S&P and the Dow Jones Industrial Average. These are the things we should be discussing, not line-item cuts to long-standing programs.

I do appreciate the county executives and the chairman's focus on reserves. They are important. Keeping our AAA bond rating is critical, and I appreciate what's being done there. As you can infer from my comments, I won't be supporting the budget proposal.

As a reminder, I have supported two budgets in my time on the board and look forward to the day when I can support another one. It just is not going to be today. Thank you, Supervisor Herity, Supervisor Lusk, Stork, then Bierman.

Thank you very much, Madam Vice Chair. I want to begin by expressing my appreciation for the extensive work that has gone into this year's proposal and throughout this challenging budget cycle. I want to also thank the individuals and the organizations that took time to testify on our budget process and share their important thoughts with us.

And to begin, I'll say I support the quarter penny reduction to the real estate tax rate, as this is an option that balances near-term relief with long-term responsibility. And we've discussed throughout the budget season, we must be mindful of the fiscal pressures we anticipate in FY 2028 and beyond.

With this tax rate reduction, this will be the fifth time in six years that the Board of Supervisors has lowered the real estate tax rate. We recognize the serious concerns our residents continue to face with affordability in this region.

I also want to express my strong support for the addition of an additional quarter penny to the affordable housing, which is so vital for the future of this county. Now, also note, this year's proposed reductions require all of us to be thoughtful about what programs are essential to safety, stability, and well-being in our community.

I appreciate that several restorations that my office advocated for have been included in this markup, especially the part-time preschool program, the home-delivered meals, and the low- and moderate-income home repair programs. All of these programs are extraordinarily important to some of the most vulnerable residents in our community.

And these restorations ensure their continued operations. That said, I am concerned about eliminating the crossing guards that are high schools. Many of these schools sit on high-volume, dangerous roads with crash histories.

However, we have new tools to improve safety in these school zones, like automatic speed cameras, which are expanded in this year's budget. We will continue to work with police and schools to ensure that students are getting safely to and from school, and we'll continue to work to improve the infrastructure around schools as they have already been done in many locations already.
Therefore, I would advocate that staff who are involved in the Eliminated Kinship Program work with individuals who are a part of that program to move them into another kinship program, if possible.

And in closing, this board has difficult choices ahead, but today and also in next year. And I believe that by providing tax relief, protecting essential safety and human services programs, and investing strategically in affordable housing preservation, we are taking a responsible series of steps that reflect our values as a county.

Thank you, Madam Vice Chairman. Thank you, Supervisor Lusk. I have Stork, Bierman, and then Sizemore Heiser. Thank you, Madam Vice Chair, and I appreciate the opportunity, and I look forward to supporting this budget that's been presented.

I always have to start by thanking the county executive for his long work, as well as the many staff members that were crucial parts of that.
